uses: Plantain is the classic wayside first-aid herb of folk practice: a fresh leaf, chewed or crushed, was pressed onto insect bites, nettle stings, small burns and minor cuts. Culpeper praised its cooling, binding juice for sore eyes, burns and old sores. A warm tea of the leaves was a traditional drink for loose bowels, and Culpeper also offered it for coughs. The Anglo-Saxon Nine Herbs Charm names it among nine sacred plants, and young leaves have long been eaten as a green.
energetics: Culpeper called plantain cold and dry
caution_pregnancy: Little is known about broadleaf plantain itself. For the closely related ribwort plantain, the EMA says safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established and does not recommend it then. Not enough is known; avoid medicinal use.
caution_medications: No interactions are reported for the closely related ribwort plantain, and we found none recorded for broadleaf plantain. Few studies have looked, so ask a pharmacist if you take regular medicines.
caution_conditions: Do not use it if you are allergic to plantain or its pollen. NC State notes that eating large amounts can cause a drop in blood pressure. See a doctor if a cough brings shortness of breath, fever or pus-colored phlegm. Medicinal use isn't established for young children; most ribwort products aren't recommended under 12, and none under 3.
caution_duration: If a cough, throat irritation or skin inflammation lasts more than a week, see a doctor or qualified practitioner.
caution_topical: No side effects are known for the related ribwort plantain on the skin, but allergy is possible; stop if a rash appears. Grieve notes that leaves are no help for internal bleeding, so see a doctor for any wound that keeps bleeding.
garden_harvest_timing: Pick young, tender leaves through the growing season; older leaves get stringy. Ripe seed spikes follow in summer.
garden_water: Tolerates compacted, trampled and occasionally wet ground
notes: Usually foraged rather than planted: it grows in lawns, paths and roadsides, survives mowing and trampling, and each plant sets thousands of seeds. Not related to the cooking banana also called plantain. Culpeper notes that other astrologers gave it to Mars, but he placed it under Venus. Grieve says Indigenous peoples in America named it for the European settlers it seemed to follow.
